content:
The report-generating process decides the answer
Under independent equiprobable sexes, suppose a two-boy family always reports a boy and a mixed family reports one with probability q. Conditioning on that report gives P(two boys | report)=1/(1+2q): one-third for q=1 and one-half for q=1/2. An unspecified reporting protocol leaves the puzzle underdetermined. This is a modeling issue before it is an argument between statistical schools.

content:
External correction is the useful endpoint
The lasting lesson is to let evidence and explicit consequences challenge a cherished theory. Published science is itself corrigible, so citing a textbook cannot be the end of that practice. Apply the same willingness to update to replication failures, to this curriculum and to these annotations.

content:
Finite agents must pay for inference
An approximation can produce a better decision than an exact calculation that finishes too late or consumes the available resources. An ideal consistency theorem does not specify the best approximation under a computation budget. Practical superiority requires comparing achievable procedures, including their costs.

quote: Not an answer, but the answer.
content:
The theorem supplies no privileged prior
Conditional-probability identities are exact within their assumptions. They do not identify the correct hypothesis space, causal model, prior or utility function for a difficult real-world problem. A philosophical conversion to Bayesian language supplies none of those missing inputs by itself.
